The AI selloff is not about demand evaporating. It is about cash flow, financing cost and how long the market is willing to wait for the returns.

Demand signals remain extremely strong.

SK hynix just reported Q3 revenue of 104.6 trillion won (+328% YoY) and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won with an ~80% margin. Management said DRAM and HBM volumes are effectively sold out through 2029, customer HBM requests are roughly double what they can supply, and they expect the supply shortage to persist through 2030. Long-term agreements already cover more than half of 2027–2028 capacity with 14 major customers. That is not a demand problem.⁠

Anthropic’s S-1 shows the unit economics at the model layer improving sharply. Revenue per dollar of compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.40 in Q1 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026 - a 5.2× improvement in five quarters. Compute costs fell from 251% of revenue to 48%. The company generated its first quarterly operating profit. Revenue grew 1,368% YoY while compute expense rose only ~300%. Efficiency is rising, not collapsing.⁠

GPU rental prices have turned higher again. B200 on-demand rates rose more than 20% in a month in some indices; H100 and H200 also firmed. Tightness in the spot and short-term rental market is consistent with the hyperscalers’ own comments that they still cannot meet all the demand they see.⁠

On the supply side the hyperscalers themselves are not signalling a slowdown. Amazon maintained ~$220 billion 2026 cash capex and said it will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027, with Andy Jassy noting that even at these levels demand will still exceed capacity. Alphabet kept its $195–205 billion 2026 range and said 2027 capex will rise significantly. Meta raised the bottom of its range. These are the companies closest to the demand. They are still leaving demand on the table and planning higher spend next year.⁠

What the market is reacting to is the cash flow and financing picture.

In Q3, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta reported negative free cash flow. Theses companies are now funding the gap with a combination of operating cash, new debt and equity issuance. Amazon alone raised substantial long-term debt in the quarter. Combined 2026 capex guidance across the major hyperscalers is now in the $700+ billion range.⁠

This is the classic tension Philip Fisher described in Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits: exceptional companies will temporarily depress free cash flow and reported earnings when they invest heavily in capacity that expands long-term earning power. The market often treats the near-term cash burn as a problem rather than the necessary cost of building the next phase of growth. Fisher’s view was that investors who focus on the long-range profit outlook and are willing to look through the temporary expense should benefit when the results arrive.

The valuation backdrop is also different from prior bubbles. The NASDAQ Composite’s trailing PE is in the high-20s today versus roughly 190× at the March 2000 peak. The multiple then was several times higher. This is not a pure multiple-expansion story running on narratives alone.

The risks are there and they are mostly about financing and timing, not about whether the underlying demand for AI compute exists:

- How long free cash flow stays under pressure and how expensive or available the external capital becomes.
- Whether power, memory and data-centre delivery constraints stretch the payback further than expected.
- Whether core businesses (search, advertising, traditional cloud) slow enough to offset the AI-driven growth in the near term.

Nonetheless the primary evidence from the companies building the capacity (hyperscalers), the companies supplying the critical components (memory) and the companies delivering the models (Anthropic and others) points to demand that continues to exceed available supply. The stocks have sold off because investors are now focused on the cash flow gap and the cost of bridging it, not because the demand data has broken.

That distinction matters for the next 8–12 months. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE

Had a discussion with the Discord bros - as people living on the frontier of the world (Internet is ahead of real world by 1-2 years) - it is clear that the Overton Window for modern society has shifted and the pendulum is swinging back to Aristocratic Era - this is just a natural, cyclical consequence of the past 100 years of meritocracy and human "equalness" we've had. It's not good or bad, it just is what it is. 

The top 0.5% of the world has already started creating their own noble houses. Elon has more kids than what's publicly stated. Chinese billionaires also giving birth to many kids through surrogates - there was the article where one of them joked "if my kid marries Elon's kids, we can have a dynasty" - he's not joking. Telegram founder Pavel leaving his fortune to over 100 children (future Kakin heir war?) 

And these people will soon set up their own schools, education systems - a16z school is already a prime example of this. We are bringing back company towns, because of the housing crisis. Honestly, all of this is just a rehash of the same history of humanity. 

What was more important to me, was figuring out what this meant for the little guy, for 99% of the world who's not interested in joining a noble house. The plan was simpler than I thought - but not a very prestigious one. It's something like

- Become self dependent, grow your own crops, have your own electricity and running water
- Move to a rural town with your friends (I believe there will be a trend of people moving out of cities back to rural towns for the ones who are not the top 1%)
- Start a new mini city 
- Live peacefully, and ignore what's going on in the rest of the world

You could alternatively stay in the city, but that would require making more and more money so you can afford the basic necessities - a house, rising costs of living, etc. 

Simply put, revert to the normal peasant back in the day. It's not complicated, but yet it's an answer I found myself deeply fighting against. It sounds like a "downgrade" to current city life. It is what it is.

Competition means profits being competed away

Any company that can use AI to reduce cost also means every other company can reduce cost and ultimately it causes margin compression

AI is not helping companies create moats - its commoditisation of the moats they once had 

Those intelligent lawyers, accountants, engineers were previously talent moats with scarcity

This is like the 2 parent working household - at the start it seems like a boom with more income but overtime that becomes the new baseline for affordability

AI is only driving more extreme competition and it will only make it harder for every business not easier when it comes to winning

The goal of a business is not lowering costs or having less employees - its long term profitability

The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.

It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.

The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in. 

Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!

When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!

I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.

The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.

The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.

ALERT🚨🚨🚨: AMD's @AnushElangovan and his team have achieved up to 2x better performance per dollar than even B200 on Kimi K3 Agentic Inference! This is due to various software optimization efforts, including tuning AITER kernels and MonoKernel decode.

Along with MI355X having 2304GB of HBM per server, this allows it to avoid crossing slow 8x400Gbit/s scale-out networking between servers, which B200 needs to do due to having less than 1.5TB of HBM.

Great work to Anush, Peng Sun, Ramine, Emad, and the vLLM team for this amazing work!
